video_title: Housing Weakness is spreading to luxury buyers | Ivy Zelman
gist: Ivy Zelman says housing has taken another leg down since rates topped 7%, with weakness now spreading to luxury and move-up buyers. She covers buy-downs costing about 900bp of margin, a needed land price reset, and her contrarian view that there is no housing shortage given demographics, though she does not expect a GFC. A second segment with gold-focused guest Trey argues fiscal dominance will stop further Fed hikes and that $4,000 gold is a durable floor.

themes.theme: Housing's new leg down, now reaching luxury

insights.claim: Ivy Zelman says Zelman & Associates' September homebuilder survey was among the weakest ever on rate of change in KPIs, with weakness continuing into October, as the industry enters a sixth year of a flat-to-down market.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Expect weak homebuilder orders and guidance into 2027.
insights.quote: we really have seen since rates spiked another leg down

insights.claim: Zelman says the luxury, second-time move-up and active-adult segments, which had been healthy while entry-level felt like a recession, weakened in September and early October as geopolitics dented consumer confidence.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: The affluent consumer that had been supporting the economy is weakening too.
insights.quote: Entry level was definitely weak and feeling as like we are in a recession

insights.claim: Zelman says mortgage rates spiking above 7% shocked buyers; weakness is now broad-based rather than regional, with the already-down Sun Belt, Southwest and Southeast under more pressure and previously resilient markets feeling it too.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: There are few regional safe havens left in new-home demand.

insights.claim: Zelman expects a slow grind with housing likely lower rather than higher, calling it the 'redheaded stepchild' in a K-shaped, AI-versus-everyone-else economy.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Housing-linked equities may stay laggards versus AI beneficiaries.
insights.quote: I feel like the housing industry is the redheaded stepchild and has been left for dead

insights.claim: Zelman reports that since late summer, ICE raids affecting job sites have created labor constraints, so builders now face labor and material cost headwinds they cannot pass on to buyers.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Margin pressure on builders is coming from both pricing and costs.

insights.claim: Public homebuilders account for 53% of new home sales and about 80% of new homes sold use a mortgage rate buy-down; buying a rate down 250bp costs nearly 900bp of gross margin.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Holding volume with buy-downs comes at a steep cost to builder margins.
insights.quote: roughly 80% of all new homes sold are using a buy-down

insights.claim: Zelman says that with rates higher, builders can no longer buy down to 4.99% (the top builder offered incentives up to 12% of ASP) and are now qualifying buyers at about a 5.5% buy-down rate.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Affordability tools are being exhausted, which threatens absorption.

insights.claim: Cancellation rates are rising but less than the 40-50% spike of 2022 because builders mostly sell quick-closing specs; build-to-order builders face more backlog cancellation and renegotiation risk.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Spec-heavy builders are better insulated from cancellations than build-to-order peers.

insights.claim: Zelman says the public-vs-private builder cost of capital gap is 500-1,000bp, along with purchasing and trade-labor advantages, and that the Japanese builders plus Berkshire Hathaway now hold about 12% of new home market share.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Scale players should gain share as private builders are squeezed.
insights.quote: the cost of capital of public versus private can be anywhere from 500 to 1,000 basis points

insights.claim: Zelman expects acquirers to integrate past deals and other public builders to hold off on M&A until real distress appears.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Distressed private builders could become the next wave of M&A.

insights.claim: Zelman sees value in Lennar on a long horizon, citing Berkshire Hathaway adding to its position and already owning housing businesses like Clayton Homes and Benjamin Moore.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Value investors are buying housing during peak pessimism.

insights.claim: Zelman says land prices must reset for affordability; the latest land development survey shows only a modest tick lower in finished lot prices, and land bankers/sellers will need to capitulate as builders cut starts; the September survey showed single-family starts down 7% year over year.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Land banker returns and lot prices are the next shoe to drop.
insights.quote: land sitting idle is not good

insights.claim: Zelman estimates the private-equity-funded land banking industry at roughly $35B, enabling public builders' land-light strategies, and expects its investors to get lower returns than promised.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Private real-asset investors in land banking face markdowns.
insights.quote: they're probably going to have to come to grips with their returns are going to be lower than they were promised

insights.claim: Builders are walking away from option deposits and renegotiating terms and even prices, while land sellers have limited room to give: half their costs are hard costs, split between regulatory/impact fees and development costs, the latter squeezed by diesel doubling.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Lot-price relief will be slow and partial.

insights.claim: Zelman contrarily argues the US is not in a housing shortage but a roughly balanced market at about 1.4M starts, and that by 2030 deaths will exceed births; with immigration halted, household formation will slow and housing supply needs will fall in the next decade.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Long-run housing demand assumptions behind builder and land valuations may be too high.
insights.quote: we believe that we're not in a housing shortage

insights.claim: Zelman says about 22% of 20-39 year olds now live at home versus 15% in the 1980s-90s; each 100bp increase removes about half a million households, and she does not expect it to fall below 20% again given changed mindsets.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Structurally lower household formation weighs on for-sale housing demand.
insights.quote: for every 100 basis point increase in young adults living at home, that takes away half a million households

insights.claim: Renter households are growing faster than owner households are falling, and with Sun Belt supply having pushed rents down, rent-to-income is now very affordable, a green shoot for the rental market.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Rental housing is the relative bright spot in the housing ecosystem.

insights.claim: Zelman says intergenerational wealth transfer mostly goes to the already wealthy: Fannie/Freddie/FHA data show down-payment gifting steady at about 15-20%, though all-cash purchases by the youngest cohort have spiked a few hundred basis points.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: The 'great wealth transfer' won't broadly fix first-time buyer affordability.

insights.claim: Zelman does not expect a GFC-style systemic housing crisis because Dodd-Frank qualified-mortgage guardrails keep mortgage credit solid and public builders are land-light with low leverage; the bigger risks are $40T of national debt and the long end of the curve.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: This looks like a painful cyclical downturn, not a credit crisis.
insights.quote: we don't think this would be a GFC

insights.claim: Zelman says homebuilder AI and robotics efforts are not yet material; D.R. Horton is piloting a Toronto-based company's robotic framing, and Pulte's 'Explorer' product targets buyers in their 40s buying future retirement second homes.
insights.speaker: Ivy Zelman
insights.so_what: Builder tech adoption is too slow to offset cyclical pressure.

themes.theme: Fed, sovereign stress and gold (Trey segment)

insights.claim: Trey argues the Fed cannot tighten much because of debt load: $41T outstanding, about $1.2T annualized interest expense, and non-discretionary spending (entitlements, veterans and interest) already at 105% of tax receipts per Luke Gromen, growing 7.5% versus 4% for receipts.
insights.speaker: Trey (Wealthion guest, gold-focused)
insights.so_what: Fiscal dominance caps how far short rates can rise.

insights.claim: After strong S&P PMI data on September 28 sparked a 'jailbreak' in long rates (30-year Treasury to 5.73%, 10-year to 5.36% by October 7, 30-year mortgages to about 7.5%), Fed Chair Warsh, Vice Chair Jefferson, NY Fed's John Williams and Michelle Bowman signaled within 48 hours that no hike was urgently needed.
insights.speaker: Trey (Wealthion guest, gold-focused)
insights.so_what: A coordinated Fed message pushed back against hike expectations.
insights.quote: John Williams said he saw no need for urgency

insights.claim: Trey notes October hike odds fell from 70.3% to 9.4%, while December hike odds are about 81%, and predicts those odds will keep falling with no further hike this year.
insights.speaker: Trey (Wealthion guest, gold-focused)
insights.so_what: Rate-hike pricing for December looks too high to him, which is bullish for duration and gold.
insights.quote: it wouldn't surprise me if we did not see another hike

insights.claim: Trey expects long rates to rise little from here and says the Fed and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent would intervene at the long end (yield-curve control) if needed.
insights.speaker: Trey (Wealthion guest, gold-focused)
insights.so_what: Policy backstops may cap long-end yields.

insights.claim: Trey frames the fiscal problem as global: French spreads widened to 177bp amid political turmoil, and Lula's shock win over Bolsonaro sent Brazil's stock market down as much as 25% and the real down 11%.
insights.speaker: Trey (Wealthion guest, gold-focused)
insights.so_what: Sovereign stress is spreading across developed and emerging markets.

insights.claim: Trey says gold rose 27% in 2024, 65% in 2025 and 25% in January, and is now down 6% year to date from about $4,300; he calls that a reasonable correction, sees $4,000 as a durable floor, and expects a spurt once Fed hike expectations fade, noting GDX has held up relatively well since the March highs.
insights.speaker: Trey (Wealthion guest, gold-focused)
insights.so_what: He frames the current gold pullback as a buying opportunity.
insights.quote: I personally think 4,000 is going to prove be a very durable floor

insights.claim: Trey says the AI buildout is sucking lots of capital out of the system, making everything more vulnerable.
insights.speaker: Trey (Wealthion guest, gold-focused)
insights.so_what: AI capital demand adds to fragility in funding markets.
